steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Algorithm" section of a Wikipedia article on algebraic-group factorization algorithms: how the basic computation works and the two-step (stage 2) refinement.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Basic computation: random element, large smooth multiple, when it factors
- Choice of A and how Ax is computed
### The two-step procedure
- Why two steps; relaxed smoothness requirement
- Stage 2 variants

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Basic computation
  - pick arbitrary element x of group modulo N, compute large, smooth multiple Ax
  - factorisation if order of at least one but not all reduced groups divides A
  - not necessarily prime factorisation: element may be identity in more than one reduced group
- Choice of A
  - A = product of all prime powers below limit B1
  - Ax by successive multiplication of x by these primes; check for one-sided identity after each (or every few) multiplications
  - naive, less efficient: product of all integers below B1
### The two-step procedure
- multiplying by several small integers faster than by their product (difference-based methods: differences between consecutive primes, add consecutively by the d_i r )
- so: stage 1 Ax with primes below B1, then examine p Ax for primes between B1 and larger limit B2
- smoothness requirement relaxed: from B1-powersmooth to (prime between B1 and B2) x (B1-powersmooth number)
- Stage 2 variants
  - difference-based = basic "stage 2"
  - modifications: Montgomery's prime pairing (1978), Brent-Suyama extension
  - more efficient: polynomial multiplication via fast Fourier transform; Montgomery 1992 for Lenstra's ECM; later adapted for p-1 and p+1

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The computation works by picking an arbitrary element x of the group modulo N and then computing a multiple Ax of it which is large and smooth. If the order of at least one of the reduced groups, but not all of them, is a divisor of A, then this gives a factorisation. The factorisation does not have to be a prime factorisation, because the element could be an identity in more than one of the reduced groups.

Usually A is taken to be a product of all the prime powers below some limit B1, and Ax is computed by multiplying x by these primes one after another. After each multiplication, or after every few multiplications, the check for a one-sided identity is made. A naive version which is less efficient would use a product of all the integers below the limit B1 instead.

### The two-step procedure
- multiplying by several small integers faster than by their product (difference-based methods: differences between consecutive primes, add consecutively by the d_i r )
- so: stage 1 Ax with primes below B1, then examine p Ax for primes between B1 and larger limit B2
- smoothness requirement relaxed: from B1-powersmooth to (prime between B1 and B2) x (B1-powersmooth number)
- Stage 2 variants
  - difference-based = basic "stage 2"
  - modifications: Montgomery's prime pairing (1978), Brent-Suyama extension
  - more efficient: polynomial multiplication via fast Fourier transform; Montgomery 1992 for Lenstra's ECM; later adapted for p-1 and p+1

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The computation works by picking an arbitrary element x of the group modulo N and then computing a multiple Ax of it which is large and smooth. If the order of at least one of the reduced groups, but not all of them, is a divisor of A, then this gives a factorisation. The factorisation does not have to be a prime factorisation, because the element could be an identity in more than one of the reduced groups.

Usually A is taken to be a product of all the prime powers below some limit B1, and Ax is computed by multiplying x by these primes one after another. After each multiplication, or after every few multiplications, the check for a one-sided identity is made. A naive version which is less efficient would use a product of all the integers below the limit B1 instead.

### The two-step procedure

Often a group element can be multiplied by several small integers faster than it can be multiplied by their product. This is generally done by difference-based methods, where one calculates the differences between consecutive primes and adds consecutively by the d_i r . Because of this a two-step procedure makes sense. First Ax is computed by multiplying x by all the primes below a limit B1, and then p Ax is examined for all the primes between B1 and a larger limit B2. This relaxes the smoothness requirement for the group order. Instead of having to be B1-powersmooth, it only has to be the product of a prime between B1 and B2 and a B1-powersmooth number.

The basic "stage 2" method is the difference-based method. There are modifications of it such as Montgomery's prime pairing (1978) and the Brent-Suyama extension.

There is a more efficient "stage 2" method that uses polynomial multiplication, which is implemented with the fast Fourier transform. Montgomery originally demonstrated this method for Lenstra's ECM in 1992, but it has since been adapted for p-1 and p+1.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Computation proceeds by picking an arbitrary element x of the group modulo N and computing a large and smooth multiple Ax of it. If the order of at least one but not all of the reduced groups is a divisor of A, this yields a factorisation. It need not be a prime factorisation, since the element might be an identity in more than one of the reduced groups.

Generally, A is taken as a product of all the prime powers below some limit B1, and Ax is computed by successively multiplying x by these primes; the check for a one-sided identity is made after each multiplication, or every few multiplications. (A less efficient naive version would use a product of all integers below the limit B1.)[1]

### The two-step procedure

It is often possible to multiply a group element by several small integers more quickly than by their product, generally by difference-based methods: one calculates differences between consecutive primes and adds consecutively by the d_i r . This makes a two-step procedure sensible: first computing Ax by multiplying x by all the primes below a limit B1, and then examining p Ax for all the primes between B1 and a larger limit B2. This relaxes the smoothness requirement for the group order from being B1-powersmooth to being the product of a prime between B1 and B2 and a B1-powersmooth number.

The difference-based method is the basic "stage 2" method. Modifications exist, such as Montgomery's prime pairing (1978) and the Brent-Suyama extension.[2]

A more efficient "stage 2" method uses polynomial multiplication implemented via the fast Fourier transform. This method was first demonstrated for Lenstra's ECM by Montgomery in 1992,[3] but has since been adapted for p-1 and p+1.[2]

References:
[1] Galbraith, Steven. (2012). Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography. Cambridge University Press. https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~sgal018/crypto-book/ch12.pdf
[2] Montgomery, Peter L.. (2008). Improved Stage 2 to P ± 1 Factoring Algorithms. Algorithmic Number Theory. doi:10.1007/978-3-540-79456-1_12
[3] Zimmermann, Paul. (2006). 20 Years of ECM. Algorithmic Number Theory. doi:10.1007/11792086_37
